## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Tirīṭavacchajātaka* (Ja 259) is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. The story opens with the verses beginning with *Na yimassa* and was told by the Buddha while residing at Jetavana [Fausböll 1879]. The framing incident concerns a gift of a thousand robes: the Venerable Ānanda received five hundred garments from the women of the Kosalan royal palace and an additional five hundred garments from the King of Kosala himself, an occasion noted in the commentary as having been explained in full in the *Sigālajātaka* of the Dukanipāta [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879].
In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was an ascetic hermit (*tāpaso*, *isi*) named Tirīṭavaccha (or Tirīṭavaccha-kumāra) [Fausböll 1879; Fausböll 1897]. Having developed higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he was destined for rebirth in the Brahma realm (*Brahmalokaparāyana*) [Fausböll 1879]. In the Jātaka's resolution (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identified the king of the past as Ānanda and the ascetic Tirīṭavaccha as himself [Fausböll 1879].
According to DharmaNexus, the verses of this text share four internal text-reuse matches with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), with its longest shared passage spanning segments §1.4–3.4 to §2017–2021 with a 0.94 similarity score [DharmaNexus]. No cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan are recorded by either SuttaCentral or DharmaNexus [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations of the work across four languages [SuttaCentral].
